title: Pipeline Hazards
summary: Why a pipelined CPU sometimes can't run the next instruction, and the three fixes engineers use to keep it moving.

blocks.markdown:
A **hazard** is any situation where the next instruction in a pipeline can't safely run in its normal cycle — it forces a stall.

- Pipelines overlap instructions to finish one per cycle, on average.
- Hazards break that overlap for a moment.
- Three kinds: **structural**, **data**, **control**.
- Each has its own fix — see [pipelining](pipelining).

blocks.subTitle: The three hazards
blocks.markdown:
One line each.

| Hazard | Cause |
|---|---|
| Structural | Two instructions need the same hardware |
| Data | An instruction needs a result not ready yet |
| Control | A branch changes what runs next |

All three are handled by stalling, or by smarter tricks that avoid the stall.

A **stall** pauses an instruction for one or more cycles until it's safe to continue.

- The paused stage is filled with a **bubble** — a do-nothing slot that carries no instruction.
- The bubble ripples forward each cycle until it exits the pipeline.
- Every stall is a fix, but it also has a cost.

A **structural hazard** happens when two instructions in the pipeline need the **same hardware unit** at the same time.

- Example: one shared memory port needed for both an instruction fetch and a data load in the same cycle.
- The pipeline design promised overlap it can't physically deliver.

blocks.subTitle: The fix: duplicate resources
blocks.markdown:
The standard fix is to **duplicate the contended resource** so both instructions get their own copy.

- Separate instruction and data caches instead of one shared memory port.
- Extra ALUs or register-file ports when arithmetic units collide.
- Costs more chip area, but removes the stall entirely.

A **data hazard** happens when an instruction needs a value that an earlier instruction hasn't produced yet.

- Example: `ADD R1, R2, R3` then `SUB R4, R1, R5` — the second instruction needs `R1` before the first has written it back.
- Without a fix, the CPU would read the old, wrong value of `R1`.

blocks.subTitle: Seeing it in the pipeline
blocks.markdown:
The result isn't ready when the next instruction needs it — unless it's routed early.

blocks.subTitle: The fix: forwarding
blocks.markdown:
**Forwarding** (or **bypassing**) wires a result straight from the stage that computes it to the stage that needs it, skipping the normal write-then-read path through the register file.

- The `ADD`'s result leaves the ALU and feeds directly into `SUB`'s ALU input next cycle.
- No stall needed for most cases.
- Some cases still can't be forwarded in time — e.g. a value loaded from memory — and need one stall cycle anyway.

blocks.subTitle: RAW
blocks.markdown:
**RAW (read-after-write)** — an instruction reads a value before an earlier one has written it. This is the true, unavoidable dependency.

- It's the only data hazard type that shows up when instructions run **in program order**.
- Forwarding is built specifically to fix RAW.

blocks.subTitle: WAR and WAW
blocks.markdown:
These two only appear when instructions get **reordered** (out-of-order execution) — not in a simple in-order pipeline.

- **WAR (write-after-read)** — a later instruction writes a register before an earlier one reads it.
- **WAW (write-after-write)** — two instructions write the same register out of order, leaving the wrong final value.
- Both are **false dependencies**: fixed by renaming registers, not by forwarding.

A **control hazard** happens when the pipeline doesn't yet know which instruction to fetch next, because a **branch** hasn't been resolved.

- The CPU already fetched instructions after the branch, guessing it falls through.
- If the branch actually jumps elsewhere, those fetched instructions are wrong and must be discarded.

blocks.subTitle: The fix: branch prediction
blocks.markdown:
**Branch prediction** guesses the branch outcome early and keeps fetching down that guessed path instead of stalling.

- Guess right: no lost cycles.
- Guess wrong: the wrongly fetched instructions are **flushed** (thrown out), costing several cycles — worse than a plain stall would have been.
- More in [branch-prediction](branch-prediction).

blocks.subTitle: The fix: delay slots
blocks.markdown:
A **delay slot** is an instruction slot right after a branch that always executes, branch outcome or not — the compiler fills it with useful, independent work instead of a bubble.

- Used on older, simpler pipelines (classic MIPS) where hardware prediction wasn't worth the cost.
- Modern deep pipelines rely on prediction instead, since one delay slot isn't enough to hide the delay.

Same symptom — a stall — three different causes and fixes.

| Hazard | Fix |
|---|---|
| Structural | Duplicate the resource |
| Data | Forward the result |
| Control | Predict, or use a delay slot |

Structural is a hardware design problem; data and control are about timing information across cycles.

Every stall cycle is a cycle where the pipeline produces **nothing** — a lost chance to finish an instruction.

- A pipeline's whole promise is close to one instruction finished per cycle.
- Frequent stalls push real performance well below that ideal.
- This is why forwarding and prediction exist: avoiding a stall is almost always cheaper than taking it.

Common mix-ups:

- **"Forwarding removes all data hazards."** Not loads — a value read from memory still needs one stall cycle even with forwarding.
- **"A mispredicted branch is free."** It flushes fetched work, often costing more cycles than a plain stall.
- **"WAR and WAW happen in any pipeline."** Only when instructions can execute out of order.

blocks.subTitle: The three hazard types
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What are the three types of pipeline hazards?**

**Structural** — two instructions want the same hardware. **Data** — an instruction needs a result that isn't ready yet. **Control** — a branch means the next instruction to fetch isn't known yet.

Each is fixed differently: duplicate hardware, forward results, or predict/delay.

blocks.subTitle: Data hazards and forwarding
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a data hazard, and how does forwarding fix it?**

An instruction needs a value an earlier instruction hasn't written back yet. Forwarding wires that result directly from the producing stage to the consuming stage's input, skipping the register file, so the value arrives in time without a stall.

blocks.subTitle: What causes a control hazard
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What causes a control hazard, and how is it handled?**

A branch's outcome isn't known until it executes, but the pipeline must keep fetching before then. Branch prediction guesses the path and flushes on a miss; delay slots fill the gap with useful work on simpler designs.

blocks.subTitle: RAW vs WAR vs WAW
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What's the difference between RAW, WAR, and WAW hazards?**

**RAW** is a real dependency: read before the write happens. **WAR** and **WAW** are false dependencies caused only by reordering instructions — a later write happens before an earlier read or write. Renaming registers removes WAR/WAW; only forwarding or stalling fixes RAW.

blocks.subTitle: What is a pipeline stall
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is a pipeline stall, and why does it hurt performance?**

A stall pauses an instruction and inserts a bubble — an empty cycle that finishes no work — until a hazard clears. Since a pipeline's goal is close to one instruction per cycle, every stall cycle is a directly lost chance to hit that rate.
